passage:
Monday. After failing the lab test, Siddharth stuck a note on his mirror: "I am AMAZING!" It felt like lying, and he tore it off.
Thursday. Awake at 3 am, he remembered what he had told Pradeep last month: "You're worn out, not worthless. Eat something and sleep." He said the same words to himself, quietly. In the morning he ate dal and rice, took a short walk and texted Pradeep, "Bad week. Free for chai?"
Two weeks later. Some mornings were still heavy. Siddharth noticed that being kind to himself helped but did not lift everything, so he booked a slot with the campus counsellor. "Small kindness first, real help too," he wrote on his hand, and went.

qa.q: What did Siddharth stick on his mirror on Monday?
qa.a: He stuck a note saying "I am AMAZING!" on his mirror.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth tear off the note?
qa.a: Siddharth felt low after failing the lab test, and the forced cheer of the note felt like lying, so it did not ring true.

qa.q: Why was booking the campus counsellor a sensible step?
qa.a: Kindness to himself helped but did not lift everything, so professional help added what self-talk could not.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel receiving the chai text?
qa.a: Glad to be trusted with "Bad week", and perhaps happy to return the care Siddharth had once shown Pradeep.

grounding: The protagonist replaces forced positivity with speaking to himself as to a friend, adds small kind acts and turns to a counsellor.

passage:
The university gym was empty at seven, which was why Farhan liked it. He had failed his second-year accounts exam, and all week a voice in his head had been saying, useless, you'll never manage.

On the treadmill he tried the trick the college counsellor had suggested: what would he say to Sachin, his teammate, if Sachin had failed? He wouldn't call Sachin useless. He'd say, you had a rough term, eat something, sleep, then we'll look at the paper together.

So Farhan said that, quietly, to himself. It felt silly. He said it again.

After the gym he ate a proper breakfast in the canteen and texted Sachin: "Failed accounts. Can we study Saturday?" Sachin replied, "Obviously."

He still had his Thursday appointment with the counsellor. Being kind to himself didn't cancel that. It just made walking in easier.

qa.a: Farhan failed his second-year accounts exam.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling during the week before the gym?
qa.a: Farhan felt ashamed and discouraged, hearing a voice call him useless and say he would never manage.

qa.q: Why was Farhan wise to keep his counselling appointment?
qa.a: Self-kindness helps, but it doesn't replace professional support, so keeping the appointment covers both.

qa.q: How might Sachin see Farhan's message about failing?
qa.a: Sachin seems to see it as a normal setback between teammates, replying "Obviously" without judgement.

grounding: The scene shows a young man practising speaking to himself as he would to a suffering friend, with small kind acts and continued professional help.

passage:
Dear Hafsa,

You asked how I'm really doing, so here's the honest version. The breakup and the bad semester hit together, and for weeks I spoke to myself like an enemy. Stupid. Pathetic. Nobody would want you.

The counsellor I've been seeing asked, "Would you say that to Hafsa if she were hurting?" Of course not. I'd make you chai and tell you to sleep.

So I've been trying. When the voice starts, I answer it like I'd answer you: you're having a hard time, that's allowed. I go to bed before one now. I eat breakfast. I called Ammi on Sunday. It doesn't make everything okay, and I'm not pretending to be cheerful. Some days I just cry. But it's gentler.

Come visit in the holidays? I'd like to make you that chai.

Love,
Zainab

qa.q: Who did Zainab call on Sunday?
How did Zainab feel during the weeks after the breakup and bad semester?
qa.a: Zainab felt worthless and ashamed, using harsh self-talk with words like stupid and pathetic.

qa.q: What small kind acts is Zainab using, and what else stays in place?
qa.a: Going to bed before one, eating breakfast and calling Ammi, while still seeing the counsellor rather than relying on kindness alone.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Hafsa would likely feel trusted and a little worried, but also glad that Zainab is being gentler and still getting help.

grounding: The letter shows a young person learning to speak to the self as to a friend, with small kind acts alongside counselling and without forced cheerfulness.
